To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) novel, deeply branching lineal sequences in the recA gene family are common in metagenomic data; and (2) some of these novel recA sequences likely come from novel cellular species.

(i) the GOS Expedition metagenomic data set contains multiple, novel, deeply branched branches in the rec A and rpo B gene families; (ii) these novel branches likely come from either novel viruses, novel cellular organisms, or novel paralogs; and (iii) these novel branches are not present in any currently available genome sequence data.

we have designed and implemented a novel method for searching metagenomic data for deeply branching lineages that we have applied to three gene families (ss-rRNA, recA, and rpoB) and that we have identified multiple novel lineages in the recA family that we have tentatively assigned to viruses, ancient paralogs, and novel cellular organisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for and discovery of deeply branching lineages that have not yet been identified by any other means.

the question of whether the GOS Expedition data set, which contains over 1.5 million DNA sequences, contains any evidence of novel, deeply branching linealages in three gene trees commonly used in studies of known and of unknown organisms.
the discovery and analysis of deeply branching novel sequences in marker gene phylogenetic trees.

we have not yet found the fourth domain in the GOS data, but that we are still looking.

we have identified a few novel branches in the rRNA and recA and rpopB gene families that are not currently known to have been identified in any cultured organism, but for which we have not yet been able to identify a clear source.

metagenomic data is not yet ready to provide a complete picture of the early history of life, but the tools and methods are now available that will make it possible to do so in the not-too-distant future.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the GOS metagenomic data set contains a wealth of information on the diversity of life on our planet.
the GOS data set contains a wealth of information about the evolutionary history of gene families and the organisms in which those genes reside.
metagenomic data can be used as a powerful new tool to search for novel lineages, even when those lineages are very deeply branched and therefore not yet represented in sequence databases.
